I want to find convenient ways to enumerate elements of an inductive type by size. Of course, we first need to prove that there are finitely many elements of a given fixed size (this does not hold for every inductive type, for example Option (List α) with a size constant equal to 1).

As a first example, below is an implementation of binary trees, in which I construct a finset tree_finset n for every n:Nat, and show that this finset contains all the binary trees of size n. (I have not used any LLM.)

I would appreciate feedback on this approach (I am still learning).

In particular,

  • Is part of what I am doing standard stuff?
  • I find the proof of tree_finset_eq_set (proving that the constructed finset contain all the BinTrees of size n) clunky. Any thoughts on how to refactor it in a more elegant way?

My goal after that is

  • to generalize it to other combinatorial classes and see if it can be streamlined, and perhaps automated by deriving an instance from the definition of the inductive type (although I would need to find a way to specify a size function),
  • to explore a formalization of combinatorial classes (I am aware of at least one implementation).

Is it a pertinent goal, or does it seem pointless?

import Mathlib.Tactic
import Mathlib.Data.Set.Function

-- The type of binary trees.
inductive BinTree where
  | empty : BinTree
  | node  : BinTree → BinTree → BinTree
  deriving DecidableEq

namespace BinTree

-- Our goal is to count them by their size, which is the number of inner nodes.
def size : BinTree → ℕ
  | empty    => 0
  | node l r => size l + size r + 1

-- We start by defining the sets of trees of a given size.
-- We will want to show that these are Finset.
def tree_set (n : ℕ) : Set BinTree := {t : BinTree | t.size = n}

-- To that end, we characterize them by an inductive construction.
-- Start at the set of trees with size zero.
theorem empty_trees : tree_set 0 = {empty} := by
  ext t
  simp [tree_set]
  rcases t <;> simp [size]

open Set

-- Decurryfy the constructor.
def decur_node (tt : BinTree × BinTree) : BinTree := node tt.1 tt.2

-- Construct the set of trees of size n from the sets of trees of smaller sizes.
theorem nonempty_trees : ∀ n : ℕ, n > 0 →
    tree_set n = ⋃ i ∈ Finset.range n, decur_node '' ((tree_set i) ×ˢ tree_set (n-1-i)) := by
  intro n nn0
  ext t
  simp only [mem_image, mem_iUnion, Finset.mem_range, tree_set, mem_setOf, mem_prod]
  constructor
  · intro htn
    rcases t with _ | ⟨t1, t2⟩
    · exfalso; simp [size] at htn; linarith
    simp [size] at htn
    use t1.size, (by linarith), (t1,t2)
    simp [decur_node]
    omega
  intro ⟨i, hi, ⟨t1, t2⟩, ⟨⟨ht1i, ht2nmi⟩, htmerge⟩⟩
  simp [← htmerge, decur_node, size] at *
  omega

-- Now we define the finset, this time proceeding the other way,
-- by the induction relation.
-- I had to use {_? : Fin (n+1) | true} to get the hypothesis that i ≤ n.
-- Only with this does Lean know that the recursion is well-founded.
def tree_finset : ℕ → Finset BinTree
  | 0          => {empty}
  | Nat.succ n =>
    Finset.biUnion
      {_? : Fin (n+1) | true}
        (fun ⟨i, _⟩ => Finset.image decur_node ((tree_finset i) ×ˢ tree_finset (n-i)))

-- Finally we prove that the two sets are the same (up to coercion).
-- I am not happy with how this is written.
theorem tree_finset_eq_set : ∀ n : ℕ, tree_finset n = {t : BinTree | t.size = n} := by
  intro m
  refine Nat.strong_induction_on m ?_
  intro m h
  rcases m with _? | n
  · change tree_finset 0 = tree_set 0
    simp [empty_trees, tree_finset]
  simp [tree_finset]
  have := nonempty_trees (n+1) (by omega)
  simp only [Finset.mem_range, Order.lt_add_one_iff, add_tsub_cancel_right, tree_set] at this
  symm
  rw [this]
  ext t
  simp
  constructor
  · rintro ⟨a, ha, x, hx, hmerge⟩
    use ⟨a.size, by linarith⟩, a, x
    dsimp
    have := h a.size (by linarith)
    rw [← Finset.mem_coe, h, mem_setOf]
    constructor
    · use rfl
      rw [← Finset.mem_coe, h, mem_setOf, hx]
      omega
    exact hmerge
    linarith
  rintro ⟨i, a, b, ⟨ha, hb⟩, hmerge⟩
  use a
  rw [← Finset.mem_coe, h, mem_setOf] at ha
  rw [← Finset.mem_coe, h, mem_setOf] at hb
  constructor
  · rw [ha]
    apply Nat.le_of_lt_succ
    exact i.isLt
  rw [ha]
  use b
  omega; omega

end BinTree

Here is a shorter proof of an equivalent theorem:

import Mathlib

inductive BinTree where
  | empty : BinTree
  | node  : BinTree → BinTree → BinTree
deriving DecidableEq

namespace BinTree

def size (t : BinTree) : Nat :=
  match t with
  | .empty => 0
  | .node left right => left.size + right.size + 1

def trees (n : Nat) : Finset BinTree :=
  match n with
  | 0 => {.empty}
  | n + 1 =>
    (Finset.univ : Finset (Fin (n + 1))).biUnion fun i =>
      (trees i).biUnion fun left =>
        (trees (n - i)).image fun right =>
          .node left right

theorem mem_trees_iff_size_eq {t : BinTree} {n : Nat} : t ∈ trees n ↔ t.size = n := by
  induction t generalizing n with
  | empty =>
    cases n with
    | zero => simp [size, trees]
    | succ n => simp [size, trees]
  | node left right ih₁ ih₂ =>
    cases n with
    | zero => simp [size, trees]
    | succ n =>
      suffices (∃ i : Fin (n + 1), left ∈ trees i ∧ right ∈ trees (n - i))
          ↔ left.size + right.size = n by
        simp [trees, size, this]
      refine ⟨?_, ?_⟩
      · grind
      · intro h
        exact ⟨⟨left.size, by grind⟩, by grind⟩

end BinTree
I don't know much about combinatorial classes, but it sounds like you can derive docs#Encodable and prove that the set of elements with size n is finite for all n.

I see what you are trying to do here :)

Did you check what Mathlib knows of enumerative combinatorics? There isn't much in there, but it knows about the Catalan numbers, and that they count binary trees. That could be another place to look at for another way to do essentially the same thing.

(Also, "currying" and "uncurrying" might be more idiomatic to non-French speakers :wink: )

@Philippe Duchon Not yet! I shall look at how classical sets are implemented.

That being said, I am not interested in enumerating this specific class of trees; I can think of a few ways to reach a result faster. Rather, I am using this as a simple first example.
@pandaman Thank you for the code, I shall ponder over the ideas it contains! Thank you as well for the reference to Encodables, I will take a close look.

@pandaman I did take a closer look now, and I am impressed by the "suffices", followed by a single simp call, as well as by the use of grind later. What was your process to arrive at this structure of proof?
I wrote simp [trees, size], and a Mathlib linter automatically suggested the style (to avoid non-terminal simp).
@Eric Wieser Oh that is really nice, thank you!

I had an epiphany: using ℕ → Type to encode combinatorial classes seems to make certain things simpler.

One (perceived) advantage is that the size is fixed in the definition of the combinatorial class. Another (minimal) one is that the size function comes ready for use on every combinatorial class. It also encodes the construction of the finsets that we had to do by hand before.

The downside is the complexity of having to play with types (the "grind" in the penultimate line does a lot of rewriting that I have no idea to handle). It might also make working with combinatorial classes tedious if coercions are constantly involved.

  1. Do you think types could be handled in a better way that avoids the ugly formulas in the proof of BinTree_Fintype?
  2. Can we make BinTree_Fintype computable? Should we want to make it computable?
  3. Can we derive DecidableEq (BinTree n) for every n without proving it by hand?
  4. What do you think of this approach?
import Mathlib.Tactic
import Mathlib.Data.Set.Function

/-
We call "Precombinatorial class" a graded family `A : ℕ → Type`, where we interpret `A n` as the
type of elements of size `n`. The size function is defined accordingly.

The main difference with combinatorial classes is that we do not impose that `A n` be a Fintype.
This should be checked at a later stage.

Note that the choice of `ℕ` as index set can easily be generalized to `ℕ^d` or other sets with
the right property. For simplicity in this proof of concept we stick with `ℕ`.
-/

-- The size of an object is the type to which it belongs.
def size {A : ℕ → Type} {n : ℕ} : A n → ℕ := fun _ => n

-- Example
inductive BinTree : ℕ → Type where
| leaf : BinTree 0
| node {nl nr : ℕ} (left : BinTree nl) (right : BinTree nr) : BinTree (nl + nr + 1)
-- deriving DecidableEq
-- DecidableEq fails to be derived. I assume it exists in the next proof.

-- Show that the `BinTree n` are Fintypes.
-- Fails to compile if I do not put **noncomputable** because of Nat.strongRecOn. Why??
noncomputable instance BinTree_Fintype (n : ℕ) [∀ m : ℕ, DecidableEq (BinTree m)] : Fintype (BinTree n) := by
  induction' n using Nat.strongRecOn with n ih
  constructor
  swap
  · -- case .leaf
    have fs1 : Finset (BinTree n) :=
      -- if n=0 then {.leaf} else ∅  -- does not work, because elaborated before I can use n=0.
      dite (n = 0)
        (fun h => by rw [h]; exact {.leaf})
        (fun h => ∅)
    -- case .node
    have fs2 : Finset (BinTree n) :=
      (Finset.univ : Finset (Fin n)).biUnion fun i =>
        (ih i (by omega)).elems.biUnion fun left =>
          (ih (n - 1 - i) (by omega)).elems.image fun right =>
            by rw [(by omega : n = i + (n - 1 - i) + 1)]; exact .node left right
    exact fs1 ∪ fs2
  intro x
  simp only [eq_mpr_eq_cast, Finset.mem_union, Finset.mem_biUnion, Finset.mem_univ,
    Finset.mem_image, true_and]
  rcases x with _ | ⟨left, right⟩
  · simp
  rename_i nl nr
  simp only [Nat.add_eq_zero_iff, one_ne_zero, and_false, ↓reduceDIte, Finset.notMem_empty,
    Nat.add_one_sub_one, false_or]
  use ⟨nl, by omega⟩
  use left, (ih nl (by omega)).complete left
  suffices ∃ a ∈ (ih nr (by omega : nr < nl + nr + 1)).elems, (left.node a) = left.node right by
    grind
  use right, (ih nr (by omega)).complete right
